title: The Leadership and Torah-Ethical Teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi: Scholarship, Piety and the Shaping of the World of Repentance

The Leadership and Torah-Ethical Teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi: Scholarship, Piety and the Shaping of the World of Repentance
This survey focuses on the complex figure of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi, one of the greatest sages of Spain in the 13th century, who combined incisive Talmudic scholarship with a world of piety and abstinence. The text sketches the formative stations of his life, first among them the Maimonidean controversy and the burning of the Rambam's books, an event that brought about a deep spiritual turn in his soul and led him to devote his work to establishing the world of repentance and ethics. The heart of the work deals with his monumental book "Sha'arei Teshuvah," which analyzes psychologically and systematically the stages of remorse, the correction of character traits and the various degrees of the gravity of sin. Alongside his ethical thought, the source surveys his interpretive contribution to Scripture and the Mishnah, his distinctive guidance for women, and his halakhic legacy, which emphasizes the fear of Heaven as an existential foundation for the whole community and not only for select individuals.
The Leadership and Torah-Ethical Teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi: Scholarship, Piety and the Shaping of the World of Repentance
Biography, Cultural Passage and the Shaping of Rabbeinu Yonah's Spiritual Personality
Rabbeinu Yonah ben Avraham Gerondi, called "the Pious" (he-Chasid), is counted among the great sages of Israel in the period of the Rishonim in Spain.[1, 2] He was born around the year 4970 (1210) in the city of Gerona in the region of Catalonia, which was under the rule of the Crown of Aragon, and died in Toledo on 28 Cheshvan 5024 (1263) after living some 54 years.[1, 2, 3] His spiritual figure represents an early and fascinating fusion of different Torah and geographical worlds, which left a deep mark on his halakhic path and his ethical thought.
In his youth Rabbeinu Yonah traveled to study in the yeshivot of northern France and Provence.[2] There he was exposed to the dialectical method of study of the Tosafists and was profoundly influenced by their scholarly incisiveness.[2] At the same time, in Provence he absorbed the ethical and ascetic foundations of the "Ashkenazi Pietists" (Chasidei Ashkenaz), who emphasized absolute fear of Heaven, the duties of the heart and bodily abstinence.[2] The core of his Torah he received from Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har (of Montpellier), who was his foremost teacher and had a decisive influence on the shaping of his public path.[2] On his return to Spain, Rabbeinu Yonah studied with Nahmanides (Ramban), who became his teacher and even became related to him by marriage.[2]
His standing at the head of a great yeshiva in the city of Barcelona established his position as one of the prominent spiritual leaders of Spanish Jewry, and he raised many disciples who spread his teaching.[2] Because of his deep fear of sin, his piety and his ascetic practices, the epithet "the Pious" clung to him.[2] This combination of profound French scholarship with Ashkenazi-Spanish piety and asceticism gave his teaching a unique character, which found expression in the whole of his Torah work.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Maimonidean Controversy and Its Formative Influence on the Spiritual Turn
One of the central and dramatic historical junctures in Rabbeinu Yonah's life was his active involvement in the controversy over the writings of Maimonides (Rambam).[4] The Rambam, whose halakhic and philosophical works aroused several controversies already in his lifetime – beginning with the controversy led by Rabbi Shmuel ben Ali of the Baghdad yeshiva some eight years after the appearance of the "Mishneh Torah" – continued to stand at the center of a bitter dispute even decades after his death.[5] Rabbeinu Yonah, as one who had been raised on the conservative tradition of his teacher Rabbi Shlomo of Montpellier, saw in the Rambam's philosophical works, first among them the book "Guide of the Perplexed," a threat to the simple faith of the masses of the house of Israel, and he was among the leaders of their opponents.[2, 4]
The controversy reached its tragic climax in 1232, when the Rambam's books were publicly burned by the Inquisition in Paris. This event, which a decade later (in 1242) developed into the burning of masses of volumes of the Talmud in that very same place, shook Rabbeinu Yonah deeply. He interpreted the burning of the Talmud as a heavenly warning sign and a direct punishment for the disgrace done to the honor of the Rambam and his books.
This event brought about a complete spiritual turn in Rabbeinu Yonah's life and led him to a deep process of repentance and retraction of his opposition. He publicly declared his remorse, vowed to go up to the grave of the Rambam in Tiberias to ask his forgiveness, and devoted the rest of his life to writing works that teach the way of repentance, ethics and the fear of Heaven. It was this turn that gave birth to his monumental book "Sha'arei Teshuvah" and shaped his later thought, which focuses on the correction of character traits and on the psychological regulation of the emotions of sin and remorse.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Architecture of Repentance: The Structure of the Book Sha'arei Teshuvah and Its Principles
Rabbeinu Yonah's best-known book, "Sha'arei Teshuvah" ("The Gates of Repentance"), revolutionized the world of Jewish thought by presenting for the first time the ethical problem and the need for repentance as a matter vital to the entire public, and not merely as the occupation of select individuals or of an elite of "seekers of the Lord."[5] Originally, this work was written as part of a more comprehensive ethical book called "Sha'arei Tzedek," most of which was lost, and only parts of it – "Sha'arei Teshuvah" and "Sha'arei Avodah" – have survived.[3] The book "Sha'arei Teshuvah" is characterized by a precise and systematic architectural structure, which divides the process of repentance into four main gates.[6, 7]
In the first gate of the book, Rabbeinu Yonah charts the path of repentance through twenty detailed principles.[6] These principles constitute a kind of therapeutic-psychological map that combines deep emotion with rigorous practical conduct.[6, 7]
In analyzing the inner dynamics of repentance, Rabbeinu Yonah presents a complex psychological insight into the question of the precedence between abandoning the sin and remorse.[6, 8] According to his explanation, there is a fundamental difference between a person who fell into sin accidentally and on a single occasion and a person who has become habituated to sin and made it part of his nature.[8]
For the occasional sinner – whose heart is still sensitive – deep remorse and sorrow precede the actual abandonment of the sin.[8] Out of the pain of the heart and the shame of the face, he easily arrives at a complete abandonment of the prohibition.[8] By contrast, a person who has become habituated to sin and has developed emotional numbness is unable to experience sincere remorse as long as he is immersed in the act of transgression.[8] He must begin with the practical and technical step of abandoning the sin physically and adopting a new behavior, and only after he has distanced himself from the act and from the negative thought can he develop true emotional remorse, grieve and confess.[8]
Alongside this dynamic, Rabbeinu Yonah lays cosmic and metaphysical foundations for the effect of sin and repentance.[6] He teaches that although a grave sin temporarily "extinguishes" the light of a commandment, upon the completion of the process of repentance the commandment that was performed returns to illuminate the soul in its full strength.[6] He also discusses the special gravity of the sin of the desecration of God's name (chillul Hashem), and makes clear that it is not atoned for by simple repentance alone, but that one must join to it a countervailing act of the sanctification of God's name (kiddush Hashem) or strenuous diligence in the study of the Torah.[6]
In addition, he presents a distinctive approach of faith toward human suffering, according to which the afflictions that the Holy One, blessed be He, brings upon a person are intended for his absolute good – to cleanse his iniquities and to rouse him from his slumber.[6] Therefore, a person must accept his afflictions with joy and deep thanksgiving.[6]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The System of the Ten Degrees of Sin and the Gravity of the Commandments
In the third gate of "Sha'arei Teshuvah," which forms the body of the book as an independent and detailed work, Rabbeinu Yonah divides the system of commandments and prohibitions into ten different degrees according to their gravity and their punishment.[6, 7] The purpose of this division is to remove the sinner's spiritual indifference and to help him assess correctly the metaphysical weight of his deeds.[6, 7]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ethical Literature and Complementary Halakhic Guidance
Rabbeinu Yonah's ethical and educational teaching was not confined to "Sha'arei Teshuvah," but was spread over a series of short works of halakhic and ethical guidance.[2, 3] These books are based on the deep understanding that the strict and meticulous observance of the laws of the Torah, together with constant study, is the necessary and sufficient tool for attaining true fear of Heaven.[5]
His popular book "Sefer ha-Yirah" ("The Book of Fear") charts practical, daily and detailed guidance for a person, from the moment he wakes in the morning until he goes to sleep, combining ethical practices with the laws of prayer, blessings and the conduct of the household.[2, 3] Beside it stands the book "Sha'arei Avodah," which deals with the essence of prayer and the service of the heart, as well as the work "Sha'ar ha-Tokhachah" ("The Gate of Rebuke"), both of which were printed by Rabbi Binyamin Zilber.[2, 3] Although in the past some doubted the attribution of "Sha'arei Avodah" and "Sha'ar ha-Tokhachah" to Rabbeinu Yonah, the literary scholar Israel Ta-Shma proved in a scientific and well-founded manner that Rabbeinu Yonah is indeed the author of these works.[3]
By contrast, the well-known halakhic work "Issur ve-Heter" was mistakenly attributed to him over the generations, and source research shows that it was in fact written by another sage of the same generation, Rabbi Yonah ben Yisrael.[2] Another small work from Rabbeinu Yonah's pen that has survived from the 13th century is "Mishpetei Bedikat ha-Sakkin" ("The Laws of Examining the Knife"), which deals in minute detail with the laws of ritual slaughter, the examination of the slaughtering knife and the examination of defects in slaughtered animals.[4]
A unique and highly influential part of Rabbeinu Yonah's public thought is the "Derashat ha-Nashim" ("Sermon for Women").[9] This sermon, which deals with the laws of immersion, a few of the laws of niddah, and the conduct of the Jewish home, was first printed in Amsterdam in 1627 at the end of the book "Ha-Yirah ve-Sod ha-Teshuvah ve-Iggeret ha-Teshuvah" by the famous printer Menasseh ben Israel, and was brought to press by Shalom ben Yosef.[9]
In this sermon, Rabbeinu Yonah grants the woman a supreme spiritual standing, defining her as "the cause of Torah and of fear [of Heaven]."[9] He explains that it is the women who make possible the existence of Torah study in the generation, in that they send their sons to the study hall, watch over them so that they do not neglect their study, receive them warmly and settle their hearts with good words so that their desire will be in the Torah, and teach them the fear of sin from their childhood.[9]
Alongside this educational role, the sermon sets out precise halakhic and practical instructions for the woman at the time of her immersion [9]:
Careful preparation: the woman must wash herself well, remove every interposition and take care that no mud remains between her toes.[9]
The posture of the body during immersion: she should spread her thighs slightly and open her arms so that the water reaches every place on the body.[9] Rabbeinu Yonah likens this to a natural and relaxed posture, "the way she stands when she kneads and arranges the bread," and emphasizes that she should not stand erect and tense but slightly bent.[9]
Guarding purity: Rabbeinu Yonah warns that the woman remains in her state of niddah regardless of the passage of time, until she actually immerses in a valid mikveh or in a river.[9]
Ethical conduct and domestic harmony: the sermon urges the woman to preserve domestic harmony and a close and loving relationship with her husband, and recalls the warning of the Sages that "children of strife and children of a hated heart are brazen, rebels and transgressors."[9] He also emphasizes the virtue of modesty at the time of immersion and in her way of life in general, which brings blessing and leads her sons to grow up to be pious and righteous.[9]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Talmudic Scholarship and the Method of Halakhic Analysis
Alongside his fame as a master of ethics and a pious man, Rabbeinu Yonah was known in his generation for his scholarly incisiveness and extraordinary analytical power in the Talmudic world.[3] He composed profound novellae on many tractates of the Talmud, which are called "Aliyot."[3, 5] Of all these works, only the book "Aliyot de-Rabbeinu Yonah" on Tractate Bava Batra has survived complete, and it was first printed only in the second half of the 20th century.[2, 3, 5] In this work, Rabbeinu Yonah conducts profound Talmudic discussions passage after passage, carefully clarifying the positions of the Rishonim and presenting an independent methodology of ruling.[3]
A second type of his Talmudic work consists of works written and edited by his disciples from his oral lectures.[2, 5, 10] The most prominent of them is "Nimmukei Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah on Tractate Berakhot," which is arranged according to the order of the Halakhot of the Rif and is printed beside it in all editions of the Talmud.[2, 4, 10] In addition, the novellae of his disciples on Tractates Sanhedrin and Avodah Zarah have come down to us.[3]
Rabbeinu Yonah's legal scholarship constantly combines dialectical analysis with ethical implications and the integration of the laws of the Torah into social life.[11] A classic example of this combination can be found in his analysis of the laws of evil speech within the Talmudic discussion of "kol milta de-mitamra be-appei telata" (anything that is said in the presence of three) in Tractate Bava Batra (39a), which is cited in his name in the work "Shittah Mekubbetzet."[11]
Rabbeinu Yonah analyzes the legal definition of this rule and distinguishes between two situations:
A matter that has two sides: if it is a statement that does not have a distinctly negative tone and can be interpreted in two directions, then if it was said in the presence of three (in public), the one who said it does not intend disparagement.[11] By contrast, if it is a clear statement of disparagement, then publicizing it before the many is a sevenfold graver prohibition of evil speech.[11]
Publicizing a person's wickedness: if it concerns a person who persists in transgressions deliberately and is unwilling to be reconciled or to mend his ways, Rabbeinu Yonah rules that there is a commandment to denounce him before everyone, relying on the verse "They that forsake the Torah praise the wicked, but such as keep the Torah contend with them."[11]
In the psychological analysis of this ethical permission, Rabbeinu Yonah explains that saying the matter before one or two people lacks public legitimacy and looks like personal enjoyment of telling evil speech or like secret flattery.[11] By contrast, when the things are said publicly before three, one can assume that the speaker's intention is for the good – so that the things will reach the ears of the sinner and cause him to be ashamed and mend his ways, and also in order to warn the general public against following his evil ways.[11] Likewise, when the speaker is an upright person and the matter is said in public, the public does not suspect him of lying, but is roused to investigate the matter and to rebuke the sinner.[11]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Interpretive Teaching: The Commentary on Proverbs and Tractate Avot
Alongside his ethical and Talmudic writing, Rabbeinu Yonah composed wide-ranging commentaries on the Book of Proverbs and on Tractate Avot, which are a first-rate interpretive tool for understanding his worldview.[2, 3] His writing in these commentaries is characterized by an ornate style, rich in the language of the Sages and in fragments of verses, together with clarity of thought and a pleasantness that encourages the student.[12] Nevertheless, Rabbeinu Yonah does not hesitate to express himself very forcefully when he presents opinions or interpretations that in his view do not accord with the truth of the Torah, and he frequently refers to his other works and quotes from them.[12]
In his commentary on the Book of Proverbs, Rabbeinu Yonah lays foundations for a philosophy of education and of self-knowledge.[12] He explains that the holy Torah is not like the conventions and political laws invented by human beings to regulate the social existence of a particular generation (a "conventional religion"), which change according to the needs of the hour.[12] The Torah is an eternal truth that preceded the creation of the world, and it has an essential, inner and eternal relationship with the human soul that never undergoes change, whereas its relationship with the body is merely accidental.[12]
In addition, he uses complex agricultural metaphors (plowing, sowing and the vineyard) to explain the need for the refinement of character traits.[13] Just as the yield of the land and the quality of the fruit depend entirely on the farmer's labor in tilling the soil, so the success of the soul in performing its spiritual actions depends on a person's work in correcting his traits and in governing his intellect.[13]
In his commentary on Tractate Avot, Rabbeinu Yonah develops these ideas and applies them to the sayings of the Tannaim [14]:
"And make a fence for the Torah" (Avot 1:1): Rabbeinu Yonah explains that making fences and safeguards for the commandments is a great and most praiseworthy act, which protects the God-fearing person from falling into sin.[14]
"On three things the world stands" (Avot 1:2): he presents a fine distinction between the expression "stands" (omed), meaning that for their sake the world was created in the first place, since they are the will of the Lord, and "exists" (kayam), which deals with the conditions for the ongoing physical existence of the world after it has already been created.[14]
"Love work" (Avot 1:10): idleness brings a person to boredom and mental illness, and the habit of idleness takes control of a person's limbs until they refuse to function.[14]
"Sages, be careful with your words" (Avot 1:11): he cites the explanation of the Rambam, according to which the sages must formulate their words with care and absolute clarity, so as not to leave an opening or room for heretics and unbelievers to interpret their words improperly and to draw false meanings from them.[14]
"And receive every person with a pleasant countenance" (Avot 1:15): a first explanation focuses on the duty to show joy and a shining face so that people will be pleased with him, and a second explanation demands that a person distance himself completely from the evil trait of anger and always act with goodwill and pleasantness.[14]
"Which is the right path that a person should choose for himself?" (Avot 2:1): he interprets this according to the approach of the mean – choosing the middle and balanced path in character traits (such as the trait of generosity, which is neither miserliness nor extravagance), which produces a pure heart and is pleasing to people.[15]
"Look at three things and you will not come into the hands of transgression" (Avot 2:1): Rabbeinu Yonah asks why the Tanna used the expression "look" (histakel) and not the expression "know" (da).[15] He explains that this looking is not sensory sight but mental visualization and deep and constant intellectual contemplation.[15]
In this framework, on the words "and all your deeds are written in a book," he offers a pioneering practical piece of advice: since forgetfulness is common in man and he tends to forget his sins and therefore does not repent of them, a person should take for himself a special notebook and write in it every day all his deeds and the sins in which he has stumbled.[15] This notebook will serve him as a constant reminder and will help him return to his God with a whole heart.[15]
The commentary on Tractate Avot also deals with severe warnings against physical lusts and being drawn after women.[14] Rabbeinu Yonah makes clear that physical death takes from a person only the life of this world, but an uncontrolled attraction to the temptations of woman may destroy his soul forever, and in this context he quotes the words of the liturgical poet: "A silly dove walks in the wilderness; she sees the grain but does not see the net" (that is, the bird sees the grains of food but does not notice the hunting net spread before her).[14] He therefore charts the path of abstinence and explains that a person should not be with his wife for the sake of animal pleasure but only for the sake of fulfilling the commandment.[14]
Rabbeinu Yonah's commentaries achieved wide circulation and became a cornerstone of the interpretation of the following generations. The Torah sage Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz (one of the sages of the Expulsion from Spain) quotes extensively from Rabbeinu Yonah's commentary on Proverbs and from his book "Sha'arei Teshuvah" in his own commentary on Tractate Avot, and his grandson, Rabbi Yitzhak ben Shlomo Yaavetz, based on his words his interpretive work "Chasdei Avot," which was printed in Constantinople in 5343 (1583).[12] The legacy of Rabbeinu Yonah, which combines incisive French scholarship, inward Ashkenazi piety and Spanish ethical psychology, has remained one of the central pillars shaping the world of repentance and the fear of Heaven of the Jewish people throughout its generations.

The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi: Ethical Teaching, Halakhic Work and the Polemical Context
The text surveys the spiritual and halakhic legacy of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi, a key figure of the 13th century who connected the traditions of learning of France and Spain. The article first examines his biographical and public background, with a critical analysis of the Maimonidean controversy and a discussion of the question of the famous remorse attributed to him over the burning of the books. At the center of his work stands the democratization of the world of ethics, as Rabbeinu Yonah turned the concept of repentance from a piety intended for select individuals into a religious duty incumbent on the whole community, as expressed in his monumental work "Sha'arei Teshuvah." Alongside the ethical dimension, the source details his wide-ranging scholarly contribution, which includes the "Aliyot de-Rabbeinu Yonah" and his disciples' commentaries on the Rif, which remain to this day enduring treasures of halakhic and analytical literature.
The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi: Ethical Teaching, Halakhic Work and the Polemical Context
Historical and Biographical Background: A Cultural Synthesis of Provence, France and Spain
Rabbeinu Yonah ben Avraham Gerondi, called "the Pious," is counted among the great sages of the Rishonim in the thirteenth century, and the period of his activity coincides with one of the most turbulent and formative decades in the history of the Jews of Spain and France.[1, 2] He was born around the year 4970 (1210 CE) in the city of Girona in the region of Catalonia, which was then under the sovereignty of the Crown of Aragon.[1, 2, 3] Rabbeinu Yonah died in Toledo in Castile on 28 Cheshvan 5024 (1263 CE), after living only about 54 years, but his Torah work and public activity left an indelible mark for the generations.[2, 3]
Rabbeinu Yonah's spiritual path was shaped by the encounter between two different scholarly and cultural schools. In his youth he went to study in the yeshivot of northern France and Provence, where he was profoundly influenced by the dialectical method of study of the Tosafists and by the spiritual and ascetic teaching of the "Ashkenazi Pietists."[1] He received his Torah chiefly from Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har (of Montpellier), who was his foremost teacher, and also from the brothers Rabbi Moshe and Rabbi Shmuel, sons of Shneur of Évreux.[1, 2]
On his return to Spain, Rabbeinu Yonah deepened his ties with his cousin and relative by marriage, the Ramban (Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman), and even studied with him.[1, 4] This unique combination of conservative French-Ashkenazi scholarship with the organized and broad Spanish scholarship enabled him to establish an independent educational and Torah method. Rabbeinu Yonah headed a great yeshiva in Barcelona, where he raised many disciples, the most prominent of whom was Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet (the Rashba), who saw him as his foremost teacher and was profoundly influenced by him in the ways of halakhic ruling and study.[1, 2, 5]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Maimonidean Controversy, the Burning of the Books and the Question of Remorse: A Chronological and Critical Analysis
A central part of Rabbeinu Yonah's public activity is connected with the second wave of the Maimonidean controversy, which erupted in the 1230s.[4, 6] Together with his teacher, Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har, and Rabbi David ben Shaul, Rabbeinu Yonah stood at the forefront of the struggle against the study of the Rambam's philosophical books, especially the "Guide of the Perplexed" and the scientific parts of the book "Mishneh Torah."[4, 6, 7] In the eyes of this circle, rationalist philosophy threatened the innocence of faith and weakened the practical commitment to the commandments of the Torah among the masses.[4, 6]
When the communities of Provence, which were distinct supporters of the Rambam, placed a ban on Rabbi Shlomo min ha-Har and his disciples, Rabbeinu Yonah was sent as an envoy to the sages of northern France.[4] The sages of France, who were remote from engagement in philosophy, responded to his call and placed a counter-ban on the thinkers and students of the Maimonidean books.[4] The dispute grew ever sharper until it reached its tragic climax in 1232 (or 1233), with the burning of the Rambam's books in Montpellier by the authorities of the Christian Inquisition.[6, 8, 9]
In the tradition of later generations, a dramatic narrative took root about Rabbeinu Yonah's complete remorse for his part in the controversy. The basic source of this story is the letter of Rabbi Hillel ben Shmuel of Verona, written around 1290 and addressed to the physician Yitzhak ben Mordechai (Maestro Gaio).[8] According to this letter, not forty days passed between the burning of the Rambam's books and the burning of the Talmud in Paris, an event that took place in that very same place and was perceived by the public as a direct divine punishment for the disgrace done to the Rambam's books.[8] Rabbi Hillel describes how Rabbeinu Yonah, out of deep shock, vowed to travel to the Land of Israel to ask forgiveness at the grave of the Rambam in Tiberias, and even declared in the synagogues of Paris and Barcelona: "Behold, I strike my face and am ashamed and regret... Moses and his Torah are true, and we are all liars."[8]
Nevertheless, historical and chronological research reveals weighty discrepancies that raise considerable doubts about the factual accuracy of this narrative:
A clear chronological failure: the burning of the Rambam's books in Montpellier took place in 1232, whereas the burning of the Talmud in Paris occurred ten years later, in 1242.[8] A gap of a whole decade refutes Rabbi Hillel of Verona's claim of forty days and indicates that the writer joined two separate events to create a tendentious dramatization.[8]
A political and polemical motive: the letter was written some fifty years after the events, in the midst of a further wave of struggles over the writings of the Rambam in the Land of Israel and in Italy (the controversy of the kabbalist Shlomo Petit in Acre).[6, 8] Rabbi Hillel, who was a devoted admirer of the Rambam and a disseminator of his teaching, acted out of a rhetorical need to silence the opponents of philosophy of his own generation by presenting their historical leader as one who had publicly repented.[8]
The absence of supporting evidence in the internal literature: nowhere in Rabbeinu Yonah's many writings, or in the writings of his foremost disciples such as the Rashba, is any remorse mentioned for the theological opposition to philosophy as such.[8]
This complex analysis leads scholars, first among them Prof. Israel Ta-Shma, to propose an intermediate position: Rabbeinu Yonah indeed treated the Rambam with great respect and quoted his halakhic books regularly, but the remorse attributed to him was not an intellectual remorse over his religious positions, but an institutional and tactical remorse.[8] He was deeply shaken by the destructive consequences of turning to Christian courts and to the Inquisition to resolve internal Jewish disputes, and by the social and cultural ruin that the mutual bans brought upon the Jewish communities.[8]

The Ethical Teaching and the Democratization of Repentance: From "Sha'arei Tzedek" to the "Sermon for Women"
Rabbeinu Yonah's decisive contribution to Jewish culture lies in his ethical teaching, which carried out a democratization of the concepts of repentance and piety.[10] Until his time, works of ethics and piety were perceived as the exclusive possession of select individuals – a spiritual elite of "seekers of the Lord" who practiced asceticism and ascended to sublime levels.[10] Rabbeinu Yonah changed this conception fundamentally and presented the demand for ethical correction and repentance as a religious and existential duty incumbent upon the entire public, from the simple masses to the great Torah scholars.[10]
The core of Rabbeinu Yonah's ethical thought was written in a wide-ranging work called "Sha'arei Tzedek."[11] The original work was lost, but parts of it were copied, printed as independent works and preserved over the generations [11]:
Sha'arei Teshuvah: his most popular work, which constitutes the gate of repentance of the original book.[11]
Sha'arei Avodah: a work dealing with the service of God and the duties of the heart.[1, 2]
Sefer ha-Yirah (or Yesod ha-Yirah): a short practical guide to the fear of God.[1, 11] Although some scholars doubted its attribution and suggested that it originated in Ashkenaz, other scholars tended to assign it to the circle of Rabbeinu Yonah.[2, 11]
Sha'ar ha-Tokhachah: another short ethical work.[2]
Prof. Israel Ta-Shma proved scientifically the authenticity of "Sha'arei ha-Avodah" and "Sha'ar ha-Tokhachah" and determined that Rabbeinu Yonah is indeed the author of these books.[2]
The central work, "Sha'arei Teshuvah," is divided into four gates of sophisticated and systematic structure [11]:
The first gate discusses the principles of repentance and its components (among them remorse, abandoning the sin, sorrow and confession) and concludes with 24 things that hinder repentance.[11, 12]
The second gate enumerates six factors that rouse a person to return to the Lord, among them troubles, old age, the rebuke of the sages, Torah study, the Ten Days of Repentance and the fear of sudden death.[11, 12]
The third gate is the central pillar of the work.[10] It details dozens of commandments and transgressions and ranks them according to ten degrees of gravity, with the aim of bringing the sinner to a precise cognitive recognition of "the magnitude of each of his sins... for when he knows the abundance and greatness of the iniquity, his soul will be grieved within him, and then their heart will be humbled."[11, 13]
The fourth gate deals with the distinctions of atonement required for the various transgressions in order to attain cleansing and refinement of the soul.[11]
Rabbeinu Yonah emphasizes in the third gate that the thought common among the masses, according to which spiritual loss is caused only by active transgressions that involve a deed, is a grave error.[13] He makes clear that neglecting positive commandments and neglecting Torah study are at times even graver than active transgressions, and he quotes the words of the Sages according to which the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave the grave sins of idolatry, sexual immorality and bloodshed, but did not forgive the sin of neglecting Torah study.[13]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Practical Guides and Their Reception: Textual and Literary History
Alongside the great ethical books, Rabbeinu Yonah composed short guides intended for the daily practice of the individual and the family. The most prominent of them is "Yesod ha-Teshuvah" ("The Foundation of Repentance," sometimes called "Sod ha-Teshuvah" or "Iggeret ha-Teshuvah"), which is a focused practical guide to beginning the process of personal correction.[15, 16, 17] The book offers detailed psychological guidance, directs the penitent as to which thoughts he must avoid, and presents a structured spiritual daily schedule for building a new routine of life.[15]
Another work that combines halakhic guidance with a social and familial message is the "Sermon for Women."[16] This sermon, which bore a popular public character, dealt with the laws of immersion, niddah and the practices of modesty and ethics appropriate for women.[16] It rests on the verse "Thus shall you say to the house of Jacob" (these are the women), and demonstrates Rabbeinu Yonah's direct address to all strata of the community in order to raise the general ethical level.[16]

Rabbeinu Yonah's ethical and educational conception took deep hold among the thinkers of the following generations. A prominent example of this is the work of Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz (the Pious Yaavetz, one of the exiles from Spain), who in his well-known commentary on Tractate Avot quotes dozens of times from Rabbeinu Yonah's commentaries on Tractate Avot and the Book of Proverbs, and from "Sha'arei Teshuvah."[18] Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz describes Rabbeinu Yonah's language as "ornate and full of expressions of the Sages and fragments of verses, but also generally clear and comprehensible."[18]
This way of interpretation is based on the understanding that the strict and meticulous observance of the commandments and the study of the Torah are the necessary and sufficient foundation for attaining fear of Heaven and ethical perfection.[10] According to Rabbeinu Yonah, as Yaavetz cites him, the Torah is not merely a conventional and political law intended to order the political society of the generation (as some of the philosophers claimed), but an eternal divine wisdom that was a nursling with the Creator before the creation of the world, and it serves as the soul of the physical world; hence its eternity and its ability to confer eternity on the soul of those who engage in it.[18]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Halakhic and Analytical Work: Aliyot de-Rabbeinu Yonah and the Novellae of the Disciples
Alongside his distinct image as a man of ethics and thought, Rabbeinu Yonah was an extraordinary scholar of immense Talmudic incisiveness.[2] His halakhic work is divided between books of novellae from his own pen and summaries of his lectures edited by his foremost disciples.[1, 2]
Aliyot de-Rabbeinu Yonah on Tractate Bava Batra
The central scholarly work that has survived from his hand is "Aliyot de-Rabbeinu Yonah" on Tractate Bava Batra.[1, 2] The book is so called because of Rabbeinu Yonah's distinctive practice of summing up the complex scholarly discussion of each passage with a practical halakhic ruling formulated in the words "alah be-yadeinu" ("it emerges in our hands").[19] The work presents a profound analytical study that combines the dialectical method of study of the Tosafists of northern France with the codifying and ruling tendencies of the sages of Spain.[1, 2]
In this book Rabbeinu Yonah discusses complex topics of monetary law, partnerships of neighbors, and the laws of inheritance and documents that characterize Tractate Bava Batra.[19, 20] A prominent example of the unique combination he achieved between established scholarship and ethical thought appears in his analysis of the passage on "evil speech" in Tractate Bava Batra (page 39a).[14] Rabbeinu Yonah analyzes the rule "kol milta de-mitamra be-appei telata leit bah mishum lishna bisha" (anything that is said in the presence of three does not constitute evil speech).[14] He dissects this rule with a fine scalpel and explains that the permission was stated only when the speaker relates a real fault that his fellow committed in order to rebuke him or to keep the listeners away from his evil deeds; and because he says it publicly (before three), it is evident that his intention is not to enjoy the telling or to flatter his fellow in secret, but that his intention is to remedy the situation.[14] However, one who denounces his fellow in public out of a desire to shame him or to enjoy his disgrace transgresses a most severe prohibition of evil speech.[14]
The Commentary of the Disciples of Rabbeinu Yonah (TaRY) on the Rif in Tractate Berakhot
A halakhic work of the widest circulation is the commentary on the Halakhot of the Rif on Tractate Berakhot, called "Talmidei Rabbeinu Yonah" (TaRY).[1] This work was edited and written by the students of his yeshiva on the basis of their teacher's halakhic lectures.[1] The commentary has been printed regularly beside the rulings of the Rif at the end of the volumes of the Babylonian Talmud (the Vilna edition), and it serves as one of the pillars for understanding the method of the Rif and the laws of blessings and prayer.[1]

Summary and Assessment: Rabbeinu Yonah's Legacy in the Annals of Halakha and Ethics
The work and Torah teaching of Rabbeinu Yonah Gerondi reflect a complex harmony between incisive Talmudic scholarship, conservative halakhic commitment and pioneering ethical thought.[2, 10] He succeeded in bridging the cultural gap between the world of the French Tosafists and the world of classical Spanish halakha, and he gave his generation and the generations to come an educational method founded on the understanding that ethics and the fear of Heaven are not disciplines separate from the Torah, but the direct and natural result of its study and its meticulous observance.[10]
Rabbeinu Yonah's influence on the shaping of the world of halakha found its full expression through his foremost disciple, the Rashba, who became the undisputed leader of Catalonian Jewry at the end of the thirteenth century and continued the conservative and measured struggle against the study of philosophy among the young (through the famous ban of the Rashba of 1305).[2, 5, 9] Rabbeinu Yonah's scholarly importance was officially recognized by Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo in his introduction to his book "Beit Yosef," where he counts the Rashba as one of the eight most esteemed pillars according to which the halakha is decided – a direct drawing on the teaching of his great teacher.[5]
On the ethical and social plane, his book "Sha'arei Teshuvah" remains to this day the archetype of the Jewish literature of repentance.[10] Through the democratization of repentance and its establishment as a general public duty, Rabbeinu Yonah changed the face of Jewish society and gave every individual, at every spiritual level, the mental and practical tools for elevation, for correction and for nearness to God.[10, 15]
